tagline: A 4-million-person metro built on rivers, bridges and a reef-sheltered harbor — the 'Venice of Brazil' — where the city already drew up a river-transit network it never managed to launch.
summary: Recife sits astride the Capibaribe and Beberibe rivers, its historic core spread over islands stitched together by dozens of bridges, with a natural harbor sheltered behind a coral-stone reef. The water is woven into daily life — catamaran tours thread the bridges from Cais de Santa Rita, small boats shuttle visitors from Marco Zero across to the Brennand sculpture park on the breakwater, and yacht clubs ring the Pina basin — yet there is still no scheduled water transport. The state's R$289-million Capibaribe navigability program ('Rios da Gente', launched 2012) planned two river-transit corridors and 13 vessels but was shelved after years of stalled works, in part because conventional 86-seat diesel boats plus heavy civil works could not close the cost-demand gap. That is precisely the equation a right-sized, shallow-draft, electric foiling fleet changes: the rivers, quays and the demand story are already there.

demand_signals.label: Metro gateway volume
demand_signals.value: 9.6 million passengers through Recife/Guararapes International Airport in 2024 — an all-time record
demand_signals.note: Pernambuco's front door keeps growing; ~9.8M projected for 2025

demand_signals.label: Carnival on the waterfront
demand_signals.value: 3.7 million revelers over six days at Carnival 2026, with the main stage at Marco Zero on the harbor's edge — R$2.8 billion in economic impact
demand_signals.note: The city's biggest event happens directly on the water; official city figure (methodology has been debated in local press, but the waterfront-scale is not in doubt)

demand_signals.label: Cruise gateway
demand_signals.value: 19 cruise calls and 30,000+ passengers in the 2024/25 season; a new R$10M passenger terminal announced in 2025
demand_signals.note: Cruise passengers step ashore 400 m from Marco Zero with no on-water city circuit to board

demand_signals.label: Water habits already exist
demand_signals.value: Daily catamaran sightseeing on the Capibaribe from Cais de Santa Rita (R$90–95 per adult) plus a continuous small-boat crossing from Marco Zero to the Brennand sculpture park (R$5)
demand_signals.note: Proven willingness to pay to be on Recife's rivers — today served by diesel catamarans and open outboard launches

demand_signals.label: A river-transit plan the city already wrote
demand_signals.value: The 'Rios da Gente' program (2012, R$289M) designed two Capibaribe transit corridors — an 11 km west corridor (Estação Central metro ↔ Iputinga/BR-101 via Derby, Torre and Santana) and a 2.9 km north corridor — sized at 300,000 passengers/month with 13 86-seat vessels
demand_signals.note: Dredging began in 2013 but the service never launched and the project was shelved by 2022; the projected demand was publicly questioned. It stands as evidence of civic intent and mapped corridors — not of delivered ridership

use_cases.title: Venice-of-Brazil bridges circuit, electrified
use_cases.body: Silent electric foiling tours through the historic bridge canyon of the Capibaribe — past Rua da Aurora's pastel facades, under the Ponte Maurício de Nassau — replacing diesel catamarans with a wake-free, fume-free glide through a heritage waterfront.

use_cases.title: The river commute Recife planned but never got
use_cases.body: A right-sized scheduled service on the corridors the state already mapped — Recife Antigo ↔ Derby ↔ Torre on the Capibaribe — using shallow-draft 12–15-seat vessels and floating docks instead of the heavy stations and 86-seat diesel boats that sank the original cost case.

use_cases.title: Cruise-day water circuit
use_cases.body: Meet cruise calls at the Terminal Marítimo and run guests on a foiling city loop — Marco Zero, the sculpture park reef, the Pina basin and the bridges — turning a walking-distance port stop into a signature on-water experience.

use_cases.title: Yacht-club basin and coastal escapes
use_cases.body: Recife's sailing community — Cabanga Iate Clube, Pernambuco Iate Clube, Iate Clube do Recife, and the new Recife Marina complex on Cais de Santa Rita — anchors premium charter demand, from sunset basin runs to weekend hops up the reef-lagoon coast toward Maria Farinha.

journeys.today: A 1h20 diesel catamaran sightseeing tour (R$90–95), engine drone echoing off the historic facades.
journeys.with_navier: A silent electric flight through the bridge canyon — zero fumes, near-zero wake against the heritage quays, and a smoother ride at river speed.

journeys.today: A R$5 hop in small open outboard boats, daylight hours only, weather permitting.
journeys.with_navier: The same beloved crossing folded into a clean scheduled water mesh that keeps running — and extends onward to the terminal, the basin and the river.

journeys.today: A 30–60 minute crawl by car or bus through some of Brazil's densest downtown traffic — the exact pain the shelved 'Rios da Gente' river corridor was designed to fix.
journeys.with_navier: A ~10-minute scheduled run down the Capibaribe on a shallow-draft foiling shuttle, using floating docks instead of the heavy civil works that stalled the original project.

journeys.today: Cruise passengers disembark 400 m from Marco Zero and board buses and taxis; the harbor itself plays no part in their day.
journeys.with_navier: Step off the liner onto a foiling city-water circuit — Marco Zero, the sculpture reef, the bridges and the basin — the port becomes the attraction.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Recife is a compact urban water mesh — every leg between Marco Zero, the sculpture-park reef, Cais de Santa Rita, the Pina-basin yacht clubs and the Rua da Aurora river piers is under 2 nm, deep inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope, with yacht-club and marina shore power for charging. Shallow draft (1.5 ft on N35) matters here: the Capibaribe silts, and the original transit project budgeted R$101M just for dredging — a light foiling fleet needs far less of it.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Beyond the city, Quanta-LR's 700 nm hybrid range opens Pernambuco's marquee long corridor: Recife ↔ Fernando de Noronha (~290 nm), today reachable only by air — the route Recife's ocean-racing community already sails every year in the Refeno regatta. Coast-wise line-hauls north past Itamaracá and south along the reef coast are equally within reach without any charging infrastructure dependency.

competitive_landscape: Recife's water today is served by tour and crossing operators, not transit: Catamaran Tours runs daily Capibaribe sightseeing circuits from Cais de Santa Rita (R$90–95 per adult, multiple themed departures); the city's free 'Olha! Recife' program offers subsidized catamaran tours; and a fleet of small municipal-delivered boats works the Marco Zero ↔ sculpture-park crossing continuously at R$5. The Porto do Recife hosts a growing cruise season (19 calls, 30,000+ passengers in 2024/25). All of it is conventional diesel or open outboard craft — strong evidence that people pay to be on Recife's water, with no scheduled water transport despite a state-mapped corridor plan. The gap between proven on-water demand and zero transit supply is the opportunity.
seasonality: Recife operates year-round. September–March is the dry, sunny high season, peaking at Carnival (Feb/Mar) when the Marco Zero waterfront hosts millions; the cruise season runs October–April. April–August brings the autumn/winter rains — short heavy showers rather than a shutdown — and the June São João festivals. The rivers and the reef-sheltered basin are calm protected water in all seasons; steady southeast trade winds put chop only on the open-Atlantic stretch beyond the reef, where a foiling hull rides smoothest. No cyclone exposure.
regulatory_note: The Brazilian Navy's Capitania dos Portos de Pernambuco governs vessel class, crewing and navigation safety; ANTAQ regulates waterway passenger services; Porto do Recife S.A. is the port authority for the harbor and cruise terminal. The Capibaribe navigability corridors were a Pernambuco state program (Secretaria das Cidades) — the mapped routes, partial dredging and station sites remain state assets awaiting a viable operating model — while the Prefeitura do Recife manages the Marco Zero crossing and waterfront programming. A clean, quiet, low-wake fleet aligns naturally with the heritage-waterfront and river-revitalization agendas both governments continue to champion.
signature_routes: Cais de Santa Rita ↔ Recife Antigo bridges circuit (the Venice-of-Brazil run)
Marco Zero ↔ Parque das Esculturas Francisco Brennand (the reef crossing)
Recife Antigo ↔ Derby ↔ Torre (the river commute the city already planned)
Terminal Marítimo ↔ Pina basin (cruise-day water circuit)

precedents.why_it_matters: Demonstrates electric foiling as the backbone of scheduled water mobility at national scale — proof that a foiling fleet can be the transport layer, not a novelty, and a template for launching where conventional-vessel economics failed.

internal.economics_status: DISPLAY-ONLY market (parked per Jaideep, 2026-07). Do not attach unit economics. The Rios da Gente 300k pax/month figure was a design projection that was never validated and was publicly criticized (JC 2022 column welcomed the shelving on cost-vs-demand grounds; Movimento Econômico has criticized official Recife event-attendance math). All demand framing must stay 'potential + existing tourism boats', never 'delivered system'.
internal.project_forensics: Rios da Gente: launched 2012, works from 2013, embargoed 2014, <2% executed by 2021, ~R$74M estimated loss, TCE-PE/TCU/MPF investigations, state confirmed shelving 2022. Stations at Derby/Santana were the only two slated for requalification; 2021 reporting described built station works as effectively ruined ('hoje são pó'). No 2024–2026 press found showing revival. Never weaponise the failure with government partners — frame as 'the corridors and intent exist; the vessel economics were the blocker'.
